question.prompt: If \(1-y\) is used as an approximation to the value of \(\dfrac1{1+y},\) \(|y|\lt1,\) the ratio of the error made to the correct value is:

solutions.explanation:
First compare the exact and approximate values so that we know the sign of their difference. Let
\[
T=\frac1{1+y},\qquad A=1-y.
\]
Since \(|y|<1\), we have \(1+y>0\), so \(T\) is positive and nonzero. Their difference is
\[
T-A
=\frac{1-(1-y)(1+y)}{1+y}
=\frac{y^2}{1+y}\ge0.
\]
Thus the absolute error is \(y^2/(1+y)\). Dividing this by the correct value gives
\[
\frac{|T-A|}{T}
=\frac{y^2}{1+y}\div\frac1{1+y}
=y^2.
\]
The formula also includes \(y=0\), when the approximation is exact. The required ratio is \(y^2\), choice B.
solutions.title: Compute and divide the error
